items.passage: Monitoring fishing activity on the high seas is notoriously difficult, partly because a vessel’s Automatic Identification System (AIS), which transmits its location, can simply be switched off. To estimate how often this occurs, ecologist Henri Weimerskirch and colleagues equipped 169 albatrosses with loggers that detect the radar signals of nearby ships. Comparing each vessel the birds encountered with AIS records, the researchers found that over one-third of the vessels operating in international waters of the Southern Ocean were not transmitting their locations.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It explains how researchers used seabirds to uncover the reasons many vessels in the Southern Ocean switch off their tracking systems.
It discusses a study that used seabirds to gauge how often vessels in a remote ocean region go unseen by a standard tracking system.
It describes a study showing that loggers carried by seabirds locate vessels in international waters more precisely than AIS records do.
It presents research that followed albatrosses at sea to learn how the presence of fishing vessels changes where the birds feed.
items.explanation: The text opens with a problem: a vessel’s AIS “can simply be switched off.” It then explains that the researchers equipped albatrosses with radar-detecting loggers to estimate how often this happens, and it reports the answer: “over one-third of the vessels operating in international waters of the Southern Ocean were not transmitting their locations.” Choice B states this purpose: the study used seabirds to gauge how often vessels in a remote region go unseen by a standard tracking system.

A.recipe: true first clause, invented aim (INV: motive)
A.why_wrong: The researchers did use seabirds, but the text never says why vessels switch off AIS. The study measured how often it happens, not the reasons for it.

C.why_wrong: The loggers carried by the birds did locate vessels, and the researchers compared those vessels with AIS records, but only to see whether each one was transmitting. The text never compares how precisely the two methods locate vessels.

D.recipe: right study, wrong focus (SWAP: birds as subject rather than tool)
D.why_wrong: The albatrosses were followed at sea, but in the text they serve as detectors of vessels. Nothing is said about how vessels change where the birds feed.

sources.what: Weimerskirch et al. 2020, PNAS 117(6): Ocean Sentinel; 169 wandering and Amsterdam albatrosses with loggers detecting vessel radar; in international waters more than one-third (36.9%) of vessels had no AIS operating

items.notes: Area: natural science (marine ecology, conservation). Key B. Key parts: 2 (seabirds used as the means; how often vessels go untracked). Every wrong option keeps a true first part (seabirds used; loggers locate vessels; albatrosses followed at sea) and fails on the aim or focus. Key paraphrases AIS as a standard tracking system and the Southern Ocean as a remote region.

band7.why: All three wrong options keep a true first part (seabirds used, loggers locate vessels, albatrosses followed at sea) and fail on the aim; key paraphrased (a standard tracking system, a remote ocean region). A single-finding report with no hedged second purpose, so band 6, as targeted.

All three wrong options keep a true first part (seabirds used, loggers locate vessels, albatrosses followed at sea) and fail on the aim; key paraphrased (a standard tracking system, a remote ocean region). A single-finding report with no hedged second purpose, so band 6, as targeted.

items.passage:
The following text is from “The Flitting,” a poem John Clare wrote in 1832. That year, Clare relocated with his family from his native village of Helpston, England, to a cottage in neighboring Northborough.

I’ve left my own old home of homes,
Green fields and every pleasant place;
The summer like a stranger comes,
I pause and hardly know her face.
I miss the hazel’s happy green,
The blue bell’s quiet hanging blooms,
Where envy’s sneer was never seen,
Where staring malice never comes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To suggest that the speaker resents having been made to leave his village against his wishes
To express the speaker’s relief at having escaped the envy and malice of his former neighbors
To convey the speaker’s sense of estrangement after leaving a place he cherished
To describe how the countryside around the speaker’s new home differs from the landscape he left
items.explanation: The speaker says he has “left my own old home of homes” and lists what he misses there (“the hazel’s happy green, / The blue bell’s quiet hanging blooms”). Even the season feels unfamiliar: “The summer like a stranger comes, / I pause and hardly know her face.” The poem therefore conveys the speaker’s sense of estrangement after leaving a place he loved, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The speaker does miss his old home, but nothing in the lines says he was forced to leave or that he resents anyone for the move.

B.why_wrong: Envy and malice are mentioned, but as things his old home was free of: it was a place where “envy’s sneer was never seen.” He misses that place; he is not relieved to be gone.

D.why_wrong: The speaker names features of the place he left, but he never describes the countryside around his new home, so the lines draw no comparison between the two landscapes.

sources.what: text of “The Flitting” (Clare, Poems Chiefly from Manuscript, 1920 edition, Project Gutenberg #8672), copied exactly (first stanza); the editors’ introduction says these verses “were written by John Clare on June 20th, 1832, on the occasion of his moving” to the new cottage at Northborough, three miles from Helpston; the editors’ note says previously printed poems “have been brought into line with manuscript versions”
in 1832 Clare and his family moved to a larger cottage in the village of Northborough, not far from Helpston

items.notes: Area: literature (poem). Key C. First stanza copied exactly from the Gutenberg text (1920 edition, aligned with Clare's manuscripts); the source line dates the poem by its writing (1832, per the edition's introduction), not by the 1835 Rural Muse printing, whose wording may differ (that edition's introduction quotes the stanza with “mine own” and “bluebell’s”). Context sentence from Clare's biography. Hard near misses: A keeps the sense of loss and adds a cause; B turns the envy and malice of the last two lines (which describe the old home's absence of them) into relief; D keeps the list of old-home features and invents a comparison.

band7.why: Abstract feeling key (estrangement) against three partly right options (loss plus invented resentment, the envy lines reversed into relief, old-home features turned into a comparison). A plain-register lyric without a self-qualifying span, so band 6, as targeted.

fixes: source line re-dated: “John Clare’s 1835 poem” became “a poem John Clare wrote in 1832”; the text is the 1920 Gutenberg edition, whose note says printed poems were “brought into line with manuscript versions” (its own introduction quotes the stanza with “mine own” and “bluebell’s”), so the 1835 Rural Muse wording cannot be claimed; the 1832 date is the edition’s introduction (“written by John Clare on June 20th, 1832, on the occasion of his moving”)
sources: dropped the Wikipedia claim that The Flitting appeared in The Rural Muse (not on that page); Gutenberg now backs the date, Wikipedia the 1832 move to Northborough

band7.why: Abstract feeling key (estrangement) against three partly right options (loss plus invented resentment, the envy lines reversed into relief, old-home features turned into a comparison). A plain-register lyric without a self-qualifying span, so band 6, as targeted.

items.passage: Economists sometimes call an incentive that ends up encouraging the very problem it targets a “cobra effect,” after an anecdote in which colonial officials in Delhi paid for dead cobras and residents began breeding the snakes. Historian Michael G. Vann observes, however, that the anecdote has never been documented. <u>Vann has examined a thoroughly documented case: in 1902, French administrators in Hanoi paid residents for every rat tail submitted, and some residents responded by severing tails and releasing the rats to reproduce.</u> Vann has accordingly proposed renaming the phenomenon the “Rat Effect.”
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It provides documentation confirming that the anecdote in the previous sentence took place, although Vann had doubted it.
It presents a recorded instance of the phenomenon, which serves as the basis for the alternative name in the last sentence.
It describes the event from which economists took the name for the phenomenon introduced in the first sentence.
It gives an example of an incentive that failed, which Vann uses to argue that economists should stop studying such incentives.
items.explanation: The first two sentences explain that the term “cobra effect” comes from an anecdote that “has never been documented.” The underlined sentence presents “a thoroughly documented case”: residents of Hanoi severed rat tails for the payment and released the rats “to reproduce,” so the incentive encouraged the problem. The last sentence then says Vann “has accordingly proposed renaming the phenomenon the ‘Rat Effect.’” The underlined sentence is a recorded instance of the phenomenon that supports the new name, as choice B says.

A.recipe: right kind of content, wrong relation (REL: confirms vs replaces)
A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence is documented, but it describes a different event, rats in Hanoi in 1902. It does not confirm the cobra anecdote, which the text says “has never been documented.”

C.recipe: partial: the job of the first sentence (PART, SWAP)
C.why_wrong: The name “cobra effect” comes from the Delhi anecdote in the first sentence, not from the Hanoi case. The Hanoi case is the source of the name Vann proposes instead.

D.why_wrong: The Hanoi payments did backfire, but Vann uses the case to propose a new name for the phenomenon, not to argue that economists should stop studying incentives.

sources.what: Great Hanoi Rat Massacre (1902): bounty per rat tail, tails cut and rats released to breed; Michael G. Vann says the cobra story cannot be proven and proposes the name Rat Effect

items.notes: Area: history and social science. Key B. Two links to the key: the underlined case is documented (contrast with the undocumented cobra anecdote) and it underlies the proposed name (“accordingly”). A and C keep part of the truth (documentation; the source of a name) and fail on the relation; D keeps “an incentive that failed” and fails on Vann's purpose.

band7.why: Key needs two links, one from the sentence after the span (“accordingly … ‘Rat Effect’”); A and D keep a true first part and fail later; C is the neighbor sentence’s job (PART). Strong band 6, as targeted.

Key needs two links, one from the sentence after the span (“accordingly … ‘Rat Effect’”); A and D keep a true first part and fail later; C is the neighbor sentence’s job (PART). Strong band 6, as targeted.

items.passage: Wanda Gág was already an accomplished printmaker when she wrote and illustrated Millions of Cats (1928), in which an elderly man searching for a single cat returns home accompanied by an enormous procession of them. Departing from the convention of confining each illustration to its own page, Gág frequently extended a scene across two facing pages, with hand-lettered text by her brother Howard flowing through the images. The book received a Newbery Honor, an unusual distinction for a picture book, and it remains the oldest American picture book still in print.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that Gág’s experience as a printmaker was the main reason Millions of Cats became so successful
To explain how Gág and her brother divided the work of creating a picture book that later illustrators chose to imitate
To summarize the story told in a picture book and explain why that story has continued to appeal to young readers
To present a picture book that broke with a layout convention and has endured for nearly a century
items.explanation: After briefly introducing Millions of Cats and its story, the text explains that Gág “frequently extended a scene across two facing pages,” breaking with “the convention of confining each illustration to its own page.” It ends by noting the book’s Newbery Honor and that it remains “the oldest American picture book still in print.” Choice D captures both parts: the book broke with a layout convention, and it has endured for nearly a century.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions that Gág was a printmaker, but it never links that experience to the book’s success or argues for any cause of its success.

B.recipe: partial: one detail treated as the purpose, plus invented influence (PART, INV)
B.why_wrong: Howard did the hand lettering, but this is one detail of the description, and the text never says that later illustrators imitated the book.

C.recipe: true first clause, invented explanation (PART, INV)
C.why_wrong: The text does sum up the story in a clause, but it explains the book’s importance through its layout and honors, not through the appeal of its story to readers.

sources.what: Millions of Cats (1928): Gág pioneered the double-page spread; hand-lettered text by her brother; Newbery Honor 1929, one of few picture books; oldest American picture book still in print
Gág a noted printmaker; brother Howard did the hand lettering

items.notes: Area: humanities and arts (children's books, illustration). Key D. Key parts: 2 (broke with a layout convention; lasting place). The source's “pioneered the double-page spread” is given as departing from the convention of one illustration per page. Each wrong option keeps a true detail (printmaker; Howard's lettering; the story) and fails on what the text does with it.

band7.why: P_profile has no band-7 official items. Strong band 6: each wrong option keeps a true detail (printmaker, Howard’s lettering, the story) and fails on what the text does with it; the key needs both the layout break and the book’s endurance.

items.passage: Writing about California’s valleys and foothills in the late nineteenth century, naturalist John Muir described them as untouched wilderness, landscapes unaltered by human activity, but ecologist M. Kat Anderson argues that this description is mistaken. Drawing on historical documents and interviews with Native Californians, Anderson shows that for centuries Native peoples deliberately burned, pruned, sowed, and harvested plants throughout the region, shaping the very landscapes Muir admired. If Anderson is correct, much of what Muir saw as pristine nature more closely resembled a tended garden, and the familiar distinction between wild and cultivated land is harder to sustain than it appears.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It discusses a scholar’s research to suggest that an earlier description of a region’s landscapes failed to recognize how people had influenced them.
It discusses a scholar’s research to show that the distinction between wild and cultivated land, though valid in most regions, does not hold in California.
It describes the documents and interviews a scholar relied on in order to question whether such sources can show how Native peoples managed the land.
It traces how a scholar’s interviews with Native Californians uncovered land-management practices that Muir had closely observed and praised in his writing.
items.explanation: The text opens with Muir’s description of California’s valleys and foothills as “untouched wilderness, landscapes unaltered by human activity.” It then presents Anderson’s research showing that Native peoples “deliberately burned, pruned, sowed, and harvested plants throughout the region, shaping the very landscapes Muir admired,” and closes with a hedged conclusion: “If Anderson is correct,” much of what Muir saw as pristine “more closely resembled a tended garden.” Choice A states this purpose: the text uses the research to suggest that an earlier description of the region’s landscapes failed to recognize how people had influenced them.

B.recipe: true first clause, invented limit on the closing claim (INV, BROAD)
B.why_wrong: The text does say the distinction between wild and cultivated land “is harder to sustain than it appears,” but it never says the distinction is valid in most regions or limits its point to California, and it hedges (“If Anderson is correct”) rather than showing that the distinction fails.

C.recipe: true first clause, stance flipped on the evidence (STANCE)
C.why_wrong: The text does mention the “historical documents and interviews with Native Californians” that Anderson drew on, but it treats them as evidence for her conclusion; it never questions whether such sources are reliable.

D.recipe: true first clause, reversed later link (REV)
D.why_wrong: Anderson’s interviews did reveal Native land-management practices, but Muir did not observe or praise those practices: he admired the landscapes while describing them as “untouched wilderness, landscapes unaltered by human activity.”

sources.what: M. Kat Anderson, Tending the Wild (UC Press): challenges Muir's view of California as pristine, untouched wilderness; landscapes shaped by centuries of harvesting, tilling, sowing, pruning and burning; draws on interviews with Native Americans and historical sources

items.notes: Area: history and environmental studies. Key A. Key parts: 2 (discusses research; to suggest that an earlier description overlooked people's influence), hedged with “suggest” as the passage hedges with “If Anderson is correct”. Section 5 checks: turn (“but”) right after Muir's view; key 23 words; options 22 to 25 words; wrong options with a true first clause and a false later link: B (unstated limit to California, “show” for a hedged claim), C (stance on the evidence flipped), D (Muir's relation to the practices reversed). Anderson is described as an ecologist, as on the UC Press author page (Associate Ecologist, UC Davis). The book is cited without a year (first edition 2005, paperback 2013).
band7_moves: dual, hedged purpose: the key names the means (a scholar's research) and the aim (suggest an earlier description failed to recognize people's influence), hedged as the passage hedges (“If Anderson is correct”)
abstract key: none of the passage's distinctive nouns (Muir, California, wilderness, garden) and no passage verb (shaping, burned) appear in it

all three wrong options keep a true first clause and fail on a later link: B adds an unstated limit and overstates the hedged closing claim, C flips the text's stance on its own evidence, D reverses Muir's relation to the practices

band7.why: After hardening: hedged dual purpose (the means, a scholar’s research; the aim, to suggest an earlier description failed to recognize people’s influence) as in c61a7c4a; abstract 23-word key with no passage nouns or verbs; all three distractors keep a true first clause and fail on a later link (B an unstated limit and an unhedged “show”, C a stance flip on the evidence, D Muir’s relation to the practices reversed); options 22 to 25 words. The draft read band 6 because B and C were each killed by one absent fact.

fixes: “ethnobotanist” changed to “ecologist”, as on the UC Press author page

hardened B and C, each killed by one absent fact (government policies; a conservation recommendation): B now keeps the closing claim about wild and cultivated land and fails on an unstated limit (“though valid in most regions … California”) and on “show” for a hedged claim; C keeps the documents and interviews and flips the text’s stance on them

key reworded away from the passage (“an earlier description … failed to recognize how people had influenced them”; was “a long-standing view”, which the text does not state); D lightly reworded; explanation, why_wrong, notes and band7_moves updated

items.passage: Kathleen Booth was among the earliest programmers of the experimental computers built at Birkbeck College in London during the late 1940s. While writing all the software for a machine called the ARC2, she devised a system she called “Contracted Notation,” which represented the machine’s instructions as short symbolic codes rather than as long strings of numbers. Through later refinements and contributions by other researchers, Booth’s notation evolved into what programmers now call assembly language, a type of programming language still used to give instructions directly to a computer’s processor.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a computer scientist, describes a machine she helped construct, and then compares that machine with others built at the same time.
It introduces a computer scientist, explains why a project she worked on was abandoned, and then describes the project that replaced it.
It introduces a computer scientist, describes something she devised while working on one machine, and then traces what that work later became.
It introduces a computer scientist, describes something she devised for one machine, and then explains why others were slow to adopt it.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Booth as one of “the earliest programmers” of Birkbeck’s computers. The second describes something she created while writing software for the ARC2, “a system she called ‘Contracted Notation,’” which used short symbolic codes. The third traces its later history: “Booth’s notation evolved into what programmers now call assembly language.” Choice C follows these three moves in order.

A.recipe: first move right, second partly right, third invented (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text mentions the ARC2, but it describes Booth’s software for that machine rather than the machine itself, and it never compares the ARC2 with other computers.

B.recipe: first move right, later moves invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says that any of Booth’s projects was abandoned or replaced.

D.recipe: first two moves right, third reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The text says other researchers refined Booth’s notation and that it evolved into assembly language; it never says anyone was slow to adopt it.

sources.what: The Register obituary (2022): Booth wrote all the software for the ARC2 and SEC machines, inventing what she called Contracted Notation; “This language, through evolution and contributions by others, is today known as assembly language.”

items.notes: Area: history of science and technology. Key C. Three-move structure (person, work, later significance); D keeps moves 1 and 2 and breaks move 3 (adoption reversed); A keeps move 1 and bends move 2 (machine vs software) before inventing a comparison. The gloss of assembly language (symbolic codes, used to instruct the processor directly) is general knowledge, not a sourced claim.

band7.why: S13 has no band-7 official items. D keeps moves 1 and 2 and reverses move 3; A bends move 2 (machine for software) before an invented comparison; B is wholly invented.

review.note: The Register URL returns a bot check to scripts; the quoted lines (“wrote all the software for the ARC2 and SEC machines, in the process inventing what she called Contracted Notation”; “through evolution and contributions by others, is today known as assembly language”) were confirmed on the Wayback copy, https://web.archive.org/web/2022/https://www.theregister.com/2022/10/29/kathleen_booth_obit/

band7.why: S13 has no band-7 official items. D keeps moves 1 and 2 and reverses move 3; A bends move 2 (machine for software) before an invented comparison; B is wholly invented.

items.passage: Once pushed to a sufficient speed, a riderless bicycle can stay upright and even recover after being knocked sideways, an ability that has often been credited either to the gyroscopic effect of the spinning front wheel or to trail, the positioning of the front wheel’s ground contact point behind the steering axis. But a team including mechanics professor Andy Ruina built a bicycle with counter-rotating disks that canceled the gyroscopic effect and with its contact point ahead of the steering axis, and the bicycle still balanced itself. Its stability, the researchers plausibly argue, can arise instead from other factors, such as the distribution of the bicycle’s mass.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes an ability of a machine, presents two common explanations for that ability, and then reports an experiment showing that the two effects must work together to produce it.
It describes an ability of a machine, explains why engineers first became interested in it, and then predicts how the researchers’ finding will change the design of bicycles.
It reports an ability of a machine, weighs several possible causes of that ability, and then calls for more research before any of those causes is accepted.
It describes an ability of a machine, uses one experiment to cast doubt on two common explanations for it, and then points to a cause that the author finds plausible.
items.explanation: The text first describes a riderless bicycle’s ability to “stay upright and even recover after being knocked sideways.” It then names two common explanations, “the gyroscopic effect” and “trail,” and describes a single experiment that undercuts both: a bicycle built without either effect “still balanced itself.” Finally, it points to another cause that the author considers reasonable: stability, “the researchers plausibly argue, can arise instead from other factors, such as the distribution of the bicycle’s mass.” Choice D describes these moves.

A.recipe: first two moves right, third reversed (REV)
A.why_wrong: The text does present two common explanations, but the experiment removed both effects and the bicycle still balanced, so it does not show that the effects must work together.

B.recipe: first move right, later moves invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: The text never says why engineers became interested in bicycle stability, and it makes no prediction about future bicycle design.

C.recipe: first moves right, invented final move (INV: call for more research)
C.why_wrong: The text does consider possible causes, but it does not call for more research: it ends by pointing to a cause, the distribution of the bicycle’s mass, which it says the researchers “plausibly argue” for.

sources.what: Kooijman, Meijaard, Papadopoulos, Ruina and Schwab 2011, Science 332: riderless bicycle with counter-rotating disks canceling the gyro effect and its front contact point ahead of the steering axis (negative trail) still balanced itself; balance comes from a mix of effects tied to how mass is distributed, not from gyro or caster effects alone; lead researcher Andy Ruina, Cornell

Kooijman, Meijaard, Papadopoulos, Ruina, Schwab 2011, Science 332(6027):339-42, abstract: the common view credits gyroscopic precession or caster trail; a bicycle with counter-rotating wheels and its front contact ahead of the steer axis still recovered to upright travel; neither effect is necessary; design variables such as front mass location contribute to stability

items.notes: Area: natural science (physics, engineering). Key D. Three-move structure: a phenomenon, two explanations undercut by one experiment (shown not to be required, which is what the paper claims; the passage does not say they play no role), a plausible third cause hedged with “plausibly” and “factors such as”. A and C keep moves 1 and 2 and fail on move 3 (cooperation; a call for more research); B is wholly invented after move 1. Key avoids the official 3.11 key wording. Replaces the Bratsberg and Rogeberg subject, withdrawn in claims.txt because cross_text_connections w4b1_07 claimed it first.

band7.why: Targeted 6. S15 structure with a stance on move 3 (a cause the author finds plausible), worded away from 6ae393f7; A and C keep moves 1 and 2 and break move 3, but B is wholly invented after move 1, which keeps it below the band-7 pattern.

fixes: confirmed on a primary page (PubMed 21493856, the Science abstract) and added it to sources

“depends instead on factors such as the distribution of the bicycle’s mass” softened to “can arise instead from other factors, such as …”: the paper shows neither effect is necessary, not that they play no part (it says gyro, trail and front mass all affect stability); explanation quote updated

band7.why: Targeted 6. S15 structure with a stance on move 3 (a cause the author finds plausible), worded away from 6ae393f7; A and C keep moves 1 and 2 and break move 3, but B is wholly invented after move 1, which keeps it below the band-7 pattern.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Ann Radcliffe’s 1791 novel The Romance of the Forest. La Motte has entered a ruined abbey in a forest.

La Motte paused a moment, for he felt a sensation of sublimity rising into terror—a suspension of mingled astonishment and awe! The deepening gloom now reminded La Motte that he had no time to lose; but curiosity prompted him to explore further, and he obeyed the impulse. As he walked over the broken pavement, the sound of his steps ran in echoes through the place, and seemed like the mysterious accents of the dead reproving the sacrilegious mortal who thus dared to disturb their precincts.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To convey a character’s mixed feelings of dread and fascination as he explores an eerie place
To suggest that La Motte can actually hear the voices of people who were once buried in the abbey
To show La Motte’s regret at having entered a place that others regard as sacred
To explain why La Motte decides to leave the abbey before night falls
items.explanation: La Motte feels “a sensation of sublimity rising into terror,” “a suspension of mingled astonishment and awe!” Although the gloom reminds him “that he had no time to lose,” “curiosity prompted him to explore further,” and his echoing steps seem to him like the voices of the dead. The text therefore conveys his mixed feelings of dread and fascination as he explores the ruin, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The echoes of La Motte’s own steps only “seemed like the mysterious accents of the dead.” The text does not say he hears real voices of people buried there.

C.why_wrong: The echoes seem to reprove a “sacrilegious mortal,” but this is how the sounds strike La Motte, not regret on his part, and he keeps exploring because curiosity “prompted him to explore further.”

D.why_wrong: The gloom reminds La Motte that he has little time, but he does not leave: “curiosity prompted him to explore further, and he obeyed the impulse.”

sources.what: text of The Romance of the Forest (Radcliffe, 1791), Project Gutenberg #64701, chapter 2 (abbey scene); copied exactly, one passage of two sentences omitted between the first and second sentences (adapted)

items.notes: Area: literature (Gothic novel). Key A. Adapted: the sentences “He surveyed the vastness ... reared them!” are left out between the first and second sentences; the double hyphen of the e-text is set as a closed em dash. Distractors: B literalizes the echoes, C turns the word “sacrilegious” into regret, D reverses his choice to stay.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Erckmann-Chatrian’s 1864 novel The Conscript, which is set in France in the early 1800s.

When [the Emperor Napoleon] passed through Champagne, people gathering the harvest would leave everything to run and see him; women, children, and old men would come a distance of eight or ten leagues to line his route, and cheer and cry, “Vive l’Empereur!” [Long live the Emperor!] One would think that he was a god, that mankind owed its life to him, and that, if he died, the world would crumble and be no more. A few old Republicans would shake their heads and mutter over their wine that the Emperor might yet fall, but they passed for fools.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why some people in France wanted the Emperor removed from power
To describe the hardships that the Emperor’s journeys caused for farmworkers at harvest time
To reveal that the narrator shared the old Republicans’ doubts about the Emperor’s future
To convey the extraordinary devotion that the Emperor inspired among ordinary people
items.explanation: The narrator describes how people “would leave everything to run and see” the Emperor and travel “eight or ten leagues to line his route.” He adds, “One would think that he was a god,” and says that those who doubted him “passed for fools.” The text therefore conveys the extraordinary devotion the Emperor inspired among ordinary people, as choice D says.

A.recipe: partial detail stretched into the purpose (PART, INV)
A.why_wrong: A few old Republicans mutter that the Emperor “might yet fall,” but the text gives no reasons anyone wanted him removed, and it presents these doubters as a small group who “passed for fools.”

B.recipe: word hook on the harvest (LIT, INV)
B.why_wrong: Harvest workers do “leave everything” to see the Emperor, but they do so eagerly; the text says nothing about hardships his journeys caused them.

C.why_wrong: The narrator reports the Republicans’ doubts and says they “passed for fools”; nothing indicates that he shared those doubts.

sources.what: text of The Conscript: A Story of the French War of 1813 (Erckmann-Chatrian; English translation, Scribner 1911 printing), Project Gutenberg #31288, chapter 1, second paragraph; adapted (place names and one repetition trimmed, bracketed glosses added)

items.notes: Area: literature (historical novel in translation). Key D. Adapted from the e-text: “or Lorraine, or Alsace” and “or the vintage” trimmed and the repeated “Vive l’Empereur!” given once, with a bracketed gloss; “he” glossed as [the Emperor Napoleon]. items.passage: Medieval medical books describe many remedies for apparent bacterial infections, but whether any of them worked has been difficult to judge. Microbiologist Freya Harrison and colleagues, working with a scholar of Old English, investigated one such remedy, an eye salve described in a tenth-century Anglo-Saxon medical book. <u>The team prepared the salve as the recipe directs, combining garlic, onion or leek, wine, and cow’s bile, and then tested it against cultures of Staphylococcus aureus bacteria</u>. The salve repeatedly killed the bacteria, and in tests on infected mice it also killed a strain resistant to modern antibiotics.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It explains why medieval healers chose the particular ingredients used in the remedy.
It presents the result that first led the researchers to study medieval medical books.
It describes the procedure the researchers used to evaluate the remedy mentioned in the previous sentence.
It describes a modern treatment that the researchers compared with the medieval remedy.
items.explanation: The previous sentence introduces the remedy the researchers investigated, “an eye salve described in a tenth-century Anglo-Saxon medical book.” The underlined sentence explains what they did with it: they “prepared the salve as the recipe directs” and “then tested it against cultures of Staphylococcus aureus bacteria.” It therefore describes the procedure used to evaluate the remedy, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence lists the ingredients but says nothing about why medieval healers chose them.

B.why_wrong: The underlined sentence describes what the team did, not a result, and the result comes only in the last sentence, after the test.

D.why_wrong: The underlined sentence describes how the salve was prepared and tested; it mentions no modern treatment, and the antibiotic-resistant strain named at the end is a kind of bacteria the salve killed, not a treatment.

sources.what: Harrison et al. 2015, mBio: interdisciplinary team (sciences and humanities) reconstructed a remedy from a 10th-century Anglo-Saxon leechbook; it repeatedly killed S. aureus biofilms in vitro and killed MRSA in a mouse wound model

items.notes: Area: natural science with history (microbiology, medieval medicine). Key C. The recipe (garlic, onion or leek, wine, bovine bile, left to stand nine nights) is from Bald's Leechbook as reconstructed in the study; the scholar of Old English is co-author Christina Lee (left unnamed). Key is the longest option here (one of the batch's key-longest items). The drug-resistant strain (MRSA) was killed in a mouse wound model, not in the cultures, so the passage says so.

fixes: the drug-resistant strain (MRSA) was killed in a mouse wound model, not in the cultures the underlined sentence names; last sentence now says “in tests on infected mice it also killed a strain resistant to modern antibiotics”; D’s why_wrong rewritten

items.passage: Using lidar, an airborne technique that fires laser pulses to map the ground beneath vegetation, archaeologist Christopher Fisher and his team surveyed Angamuco, a city in western Mexico that the Purépecha people built and that flourished between about 1000 and 1350 CE. The resulting maps revealed some 40,000 building foundations, or about as many buildings as Manhattan has today. The discovery indicates that Angamuco was far larger than researchers had believed, and it suggests that much about the ancient cities of the Americas remains unknown.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a technique archaeologists use, then explains why that technique has replaced older methods of excavation.
It describes how researchers learned the extent of an ancient city, then considers what that discovery suggests.
It summarizes a disagreement about when an ancient city was built, then presents evidence that settles the disagreement.
It describes how researchers mapped an ancient city, then explains why the city was eventually abandoned.
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe how Fisher’s team used lidar to map Angamuco and found “some 40,000 building foundations.” The last sentence considers what this means: “The discovery indicates that Angamuco was far larger than researchers had believed, and it suggests that much about the ancient cities of the Americas remains unknown.” Choice B describes this structure.

A.recipe: wholly wrong template (INV: method vs alternative method)
A.why_wrong: The text explains what lidar does but never compares it with excavation or says it has replaced older methods.

C.recipe: wholly wrong template (INV: debate and resolution)
C.why_wrong: The text gives the city’s dates without any disagreement about them; the discovery concerns the city’s size.

D.why_wrong: The text does describe how the city was mapped, but it says nothing about why Angamuco was abandoned.

sources.what: Angamuco (Purépecha) lidar survey led by Christopher Fisher: about 40,000 buildings over 26 square kilometers, roughly the number in Manhattan; earliest date about 900 CE, peak 1000 to 1350 CE; Fisher: “we know so little about the archaeological universe in the Americas”
the city occupied 26 square kilometers of land instead of 13 square kilometers (premise of “far larger than researchers had believed”)

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. Key B. “Far larger than researchers had believed” rests on reports that the city covered about 26 square kilometers rather than the 13 previously assumed; western Mexico (Michoacán) left general. Avoids the official 2.2 frame (“This finding not only ... but also”).

fixes: “occupied from about 900 to 1350 CE” changed to “that flourished between about 1000 and 1350 CE”, the period the source gives (it gives no end of occupation); clause attached to “city”

items.passage: In his 1898 book To-morrow: A Peaceful Path to Real Reform, British reformer Ebenezer Howard proposed a new kind of town, the “garden city,” that would combine the advantages of city and countryside. Such a town would be planned in advance, with residential districts separated from industry, the whole surrounded by a permanent belt of agricultural land, and profits from the land reinvested for the benefit of its residents. In 1903, a company purchased an estate in Hertfordshire, England, to build Letchworth, the first garden city, and architects Raymond Unwin and Barry Parker designed its layout according to Howard’s principles.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It outlines a set of ideas about how towns should be organized, then describes a town designed with those ideas in mind.
It describes a disagreement between a reformer and two architects, then explains how that disagreement shaped a town’s design.
It summarizes the problems of crowded industrial cities, then argues that farming villages offer a better way of life.
It presents a reformer’s proposal for a new kind of town, then explains why the first attempt to build one failed.
items.explanation: The first two sentences set out Howard’s ideas for a “garden city”: a planned town combining “the advantages of city and countryside,” with “residential districts separated from industry” and a “permanent belt of agricultural land.” The last sentence describes Letchworth, “the first garden city,” whose layout was designed “according to Howard’s principles.” Choice A describes this structure.

B.recipe: wholly wrong template (STANCE: agreement turned into disagreement)
B.why_wrong: Unwin and Parker designed Letchworth “according to Howard’s principles”; the text describes no disagreement between them and Howard.

C.why_wrong: The text does not list the problems of industrial cities, and Howard’s garden city combines city and countryside rather than favoring farming villages.

D.why_wrong: The text does present Howard’s proposal, but it reports that Letchworth was built as the first garden city; it never says the attempt failed.

sources.what: Letchworth: Ebenezer Howard's 1898 To-morrow: A Peaceful Path to Real Reform; first garden city; First Garden City Ltd founded 1903 and bought the estate; Unwin and Parker won the 1904 layout competition; belt of open countryside, industry kept separate from homes, profits for residents

items.notes: Area: history and humanities (urban planning). Key A. Medium pattern: D keeps move 1 and breaks move 2; B and C are wholly wrong templates. Replaces the Westerkamp subject, withdrawn in claims.txt because another w4 writer claimed it first.

items.passage: Historians studying the lives of enslaved people in colonial Louisiana have long faced a practical obstacle: the relevant records, many written in French or Spanish, are scattered among parish courthouses in Louisiana and archives in France, Spain, and Texas. Over fifteen years, historian Gwendolyn Midlo Hall gathered information from these documents into a searchable database covering more than 100,000 people enslaved in Louisiana between 1719 and 1820. Each entry records details such as a person’s name, age, occupation, and African ethnicity or place of origin, allowing researchers to study enslaved people as individuals.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It identifies a gap in historians’ knowledge of a period, then explains why that gap is unlikely ever to be filled.
It describes a historian’s method for analyzing old documents, then presents criticisms that other historians have made of it.
It explains why a body of historical evidence was hard to use, then describes how one historian made that evidence easier to study.
It explains why a body of historical evidence was hard to use, then argues that historians should turn to other kinds of sources instead.
items.explanation: The first sentence describes the obstacle: records about enslaved people in colonial Louisiana “are scattered among parish courthouses in Louisiana and archives in France, Spain, and Texas.” The rest of the text describes Hall’s response, a “searchable database covering more than 100,000 people” that allows “researchers to study enslaved people as individuals.” Choice C describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The text describes records that were hard to use, and it goes on to show how Hall made them usable, not that the problem cannot be solved.

B.recipe: wholly wrong template (INV: method then critique)
B.why_wrong: The text describes Hall’s database but mentions no criticism of it by other historians.

D.why_wrong: The text does explain why the records were hard to use, but Hall gathers those same records into a database rather than abandoning them for other sources.

sources.what: Gwendolyn Midlo Hall: Louisiana Slave Database 1719–1820, more than 100,000 individuals, 15 years of work; records from Pointe Coupee and other parish courthouses and archives in France, Spain and Texas; fields include name, gender, age, occupation, family relationships, ethnicity, place of origin

items.notes: Area: history. Key C. Medium pattern: D keeps move 1 and reverses move 2; A and B fail from the start. Key worded away from the official 2.16 key (“a problem that arises in research ... a historian’s approach”).

items.passage:
The following text is from Edwin Arlington Robinson’s 1897 poetry collection The Children of the Night.

Dear friends, reproach me not for what I do,
Nor counsel me, nor pity me; nor say
That I am wearing half my life away
For bubble-work that only fools pursue.
And if my bubbles be too small for you,
Blow bigger then your own: the games we play
To fill the frittered minutes of a day,
Good glasses are to read the spirit through.
And whoso reads may get him some shrewd skill;
And some unprofitable scorn resign,
To praise the very thing that he deplores;
So, friends (dear friends), remember, if you will,
The shame I win for singing is all mine,
The gold I miss for dreaming is all yours.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker questions the values of his friends, then predicts that they will come to regret their own choices.
The speaker admits that his work has little worth, then asks his friends for advice about how to improve it.
The speaker recalls a childhood game he once played with his friends, then explains what that game taught him about life.
The speaker rejects his friends’ disapproval of his way of life, then affirms that he willingly accepts its costs.
items.explanation: The speaker opens by telling his friends not to reproach, counsel, or pity him, or to say “That I am wearing half my life away / For bubble-work that only fools pursue.” After defending such “games,” he closes by accepting the price of his choice: “The shame I win for singing is all mine, / The gold I miss for dreaming is all yours.” Choice D describes this structure: he rejects their disapproval, then affirms that he accepts what his way of life costs him.

A.recipe: first move stretched, second invented (STANCE, INV)
A.why_wrong: The speaker suggests that his friends’ pursuits are games too, but he never predicts that they will regret their choices; he ends by accepting his own costs.

B.why_wrong: Calling his poetry “bubble-work” is his friends’ view, which he rejects, and he explicitly tells them “Nor counsel me,” so he is not asking for advice.

C.why_wrong: The bubbles and “games we play” are figures for how people spend their lives; the speaker does not recall an actual childhood game.

sources.what: text of “Dear Friends” in The Children of the Night (Robinson, 1897), Project Gutenberg #313, copied exactly (double space after a colon normalized)

items.notes: Area: literature (poem, sonnet). Key D. The whole sonnet is used because the template needs both the opening rebuttal and the closing commitment; at 129 words with the attribution it runs above the single model's 100, a deliberate trade-off (cutting interior lines would break the sonnet). The source line names the collection because the poem may first have appeared in Robinson's 1896 The Torrent and the Night Before.

review.note: Whole sonnet kept at 129 words against the single model’s 100: official medium items 2.19 and 2.22 also run 129, and the structure answer needs both the opening rebuttal and the closing couplet, so cutting lines would break the item. Writer note corrected from 123 to 129 words (notes only).

items.passage: Why have Swiss cheeses such as Emmentaler been developing fewer of their characteristic holes in recent years? The holes form as gas released by bacteria accumulates in the cheese during ripening, but the gas requires locations where it can begin to collect. Using computed tomography scans to follow cheeses through 130 days of ripening, researchers at the Swiss research institutions Agroscope and Empa determined that tiny particles of hay in the milk serve as these starting points. Because modern milking machines now transfer milk directly into enclosed tanks, far fewer hay particles end up in it, and consequently fewer holes form.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text presents a long-standing theory about a food, then describes evidence that has led researchers to reject it.
The text raises a question about a change in a food, then offers an explanation drawn from researchers’ findings.
The text describes how a food is produced, then compares that process with the way the food was made in earlier centuries.
The text raises a question about a change in a food, then explains why researchers have so far been unable to answer it.
items.explanation: The text opens with a question: “Why have Swiss cheeses such as Emmentaler been developing fewer of their characteristic holes in recent years?” It then answers it with the findings of researchers at Agroscope and Empa: hay particles in milk are the starting points for holes, and because milking machines now “transfer milk directly into enclosed tanks,” fewer particles reach it, “and consequently fewer holes form.” Choice B describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The text does not present a long-standing theory or show one being rejected; it explains what the researchers found.

C.why_wrong: The text says a little about how holes form and how milk is collected now, but it never describes how the cheese was made in earlier centuries.

D.why_wrong: The text does raise a question about a change in the cheese, but it goes on to answer it rather than saying researchers have been unable to.

sources.what: Agroscope and Empa (2015): hay particles in milk responsible for holes in Swiss cheese; fewer holes in recent years because milk goes through modern milking machines directly into large tanks; ripening tracked over 130 days by CT scanning

items.notes: Area: natural science (food science). Key B. That gas from bacteria fills the holes is general knowledge, not a sourced claim. Medium pattern: D keeps the opening question and reverses the answer move.

items.passage: <u>Kleptoplasty occurs when an organism that eats algae keeps the algae’s chloroplasts—the structures that carry out photosynthesis—alive and working inside its own cells</u>. Among animals, this ability was long known only in certain sea slugs. In 2019, however, biologist Niels Van Steenkiste and colleagues reported that two species of tiny marine flatworms, including Baicalellia solaris, retain chloroplasts taken from diatoms, a type of alga, and that the stolen chloroplasts continued to photosynthesize for a time even when the worms were deprived of food in the laboratory.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It explains a term that is central to the discussion that follows.
It presents a finding that the rest of the text calls into question.
It describes a method used in the study discussed later in the text.
It identifies a problem that the researchers in the text set out to solve.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence explains what the term kleptoplasty means: an organism keeps the chloroplasts of the algae it eats “alive and working inside its own cells.” The rest of the text discusses this process, first in sea slugs and then in the flatworms studied by Van Steenkiste and colleagues. The sentence therefore explains a term central to the discussion that follows, as choice A says.

B.recipe: sibling label (REL: claim that is challenged)
B.why_wrong: The text does challenge the idea that only sea slugs can do this, but that idea is in the second sentence; the definition in the underlined sentence is not questioned.

C.why_wrong: The underlined sentence describes something organisms do, not a technique the researchers used in their study.

D.why_wrong: Kleptoplasty is the process the text discusses, not a problem that the researchers were trying to solve.

sources.what: Van Steenkiste et al. 2019, Science Advances: sea slugs previously the only animals known to sequester functional algal plastids (kleptoplasty); flatworms Baicalellia solaris and Pogaina paranygulgus hold plastids stolen from diatoms; photosynthetic activity and short-term retention in starved worms

items.notes: Area: natural science (biology). Key A. Underlined first sentence, as in the official 2.3, with the key worded away from its key (“defines a phenomenon that is discussed in the text”). B is the closest trap: the text does overturn a view, but not the one in the underlined sentence.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Eleanor Hallowell Abbott’s 1910 novel Molly Make-Believe. Carl Stanton is bedridden with rheumatism, a painful illness.

The morning was as dark and cold as city snow could make it—a dingy whirl at the window; a smoky gust through the fireplace; a shadow black as a bear’s cave under the table.

Packed into his pudgy pillows like a fragile piece of china instead of a human being Carl Stanton lay and cursed the brutal Northern winter.

<u>Between his sturdy, restive shoulders the rheumatism snarled and clawed like some utterly frenzied animal trying to gnaw-gnaw-gnaw its way out.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that Stanton is frightened by an animal that has gotten into his room.
It indicates that the cold winter weather is what caused Stanton’s illness.
It emphasizes how severe Stanton’s pain is.
It shows that Stanton is too restless to stay in bed.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence compares Stanton’s rheumatism to “some utterly frenzied animal” that “snarled and clawed” and was “trying to gnaw-gnaw-gnaw its way out.” This comparison emphasizes how severe his pain is, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The animal is only a comparison for the pain of Stanton’s rheumatism; there is no real animal in his room.

B.why_wrong: Stanton curses “the brutal Northern winter,” but the underlined sentence describes his pain, not what caused his illness.

D.why_wrong: His shoulders are called “restive,” but the sentence is about the pain in them, and Stanton is described lying in bed “like a fragile piece of china,” not trying to get up.

sources.what: text of Molly Make-Believe (Abbott; Century Co., copyright 1910), Project Gutenberg #18665, opening of chapter I; adapted (one sentence omitted after the first sentence)

items.notes: Area: literature (novel). Key C. Adapted: the sentence “Nothing in all the cavernous room ... grape-fruit.” is left out; the e-text's double hyphen is set as a closed em dash; paragraphs as in the source. Context sentence glosses rheumatism and sets the scene.

items.passage:
The following text is from John Fox Jr.’s 1903 novel The Little Shepherd of Kingdom Come. Chad, an orphaned boy, has just woken on a hillside beside his dog, Jack.

The sun was dropping fast, the ravines were filling with blue shadows, luminous and misty, and a far drowsy tinkling from the valley told him that cows were starting homeward. From habit, he sprang quickly to his feet, but, sharply conscious on a sudden, dropped slowly back to the moss again, <u>while Jack, who had started down the spur [ridge], circled back to see what the matter was, and stood with uplifted foot, much puzzled.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that Jack is eager to leave Chad behind on the hillside.
It conveys the dog’s confusion when Chad does not follow his usual routine.
It explains why Chad decides not to bring the cows home that evening.
It describes how Jack helps Chad find his way back down from the hillside at sunset.
items.explanation: When Chad hears that “cows were starting homeward,” he jumps up out of habit but then drops “slowly back to the moss again.” The underlined portion shows Jack’s reaction: he “circled back to see what the matter was” and “stood with uplifted foot, much puzzled.” It conveys the dog’s confusion when Chad breaks his usual routine, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: Jack starts down the ridge but then “circled back to see what the matter was,” so he is concerned about Chad, not eager to leave him.

C.why_wrong: The underlined portion is about Jack, not Chad, and the text never explains Chad’s reasons for sitting back down.

D.why_wrong: Jack does not lead Chad anywhere; he stops and stands “much puzzled.”

sources.what: text of The Little Shepherd of Kingdom Come (Fox, 1903), Project Gutenberg #2059, chapter 1; copied exactly from “The sun was dropping fast” to “much puzzled”, with a bracketed gloss

items.notes: Area: literature (novel). Key B. Context sentence avoids the plague detail; “spur” glossed as [ridge]. The habit is the evening task of bringing the cows home, which Chad remembers he no longer has a home to go to; the item only needs the dog's puzzlement.

fixes: context sentence said Chad “has fallen asleep”, but the excerpt shows him awake; now “has just woken on a hillside beside his dog, Jack”

items.passage: Artist Mary Blair helped shape the look of several classic Disney animated films, receiving credit for color styling on Cinderella (1950), Alice in Wonderland (1951), and Peter Pan (1953). Her paintings, known for bold and unexpected combinations of color, also influenced Disney’s theme parks: the company asked her to help design It’s a Small World, an attraction first created for the 1964 New York World’s Fair. Blair illustrated children’s books as well, and several of them, including I Can Fly, remain in print today. In 1991, Disney honored her as a Disney Legend.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To present an overview of Blair’s varied work and its lasting impact
To explain how Blair’s travels influenced the colors used in Disney’s films
To argue that Blair deserved more credit for Disney’s success than she received
To compare Blair’s work on animated films with her work as a book illustrator
items.explanation: The text describes several kinds of work Blair did: color styling for films such as Cinderella, design work on It’s a Small World, and children’s books such as I Can Fly. It also notes that some of her books “remain in print today” and that Disney “honored her as a Disney Legend.” The text therefore gives an overview of her varied work and its lasting impact, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The text never mentions Blair’s travels or explains where her color choices came from.

C.why_wrong: The text reports the credit and honors Blair received; it does not argue that she deserved more.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions both her film work and her books but never compares them.

sources.what: Mary Blair: color styling credits on Cinderella (1950), Alice in Wonderland (1951), Peter Pan (1953); asked to work on It's a Small World (1964 New York World's Fair); I Can Fly still in print; Disney Legend 1991; bold color design

items.passage: Painter Laura Wheeler Waring (1887–1948) taught for more than thirty years at what is now Cheyney University of Pennsylvania, where she established the school’s art and music departments. In 1914, a travel scholarship enabled her to study art in Paris. Waring became best known for her portraits. The Harmon Foundation commissioned her to paint prominent African Americans, and she selected many figures associated with the Harlem Renaissance, including singer Marian Anderson and writer James Weldon Johnson. Several of her portraits are now in the collection of the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why Waring chose to study art in Paris instead of in the United States
To argue that Waring’s portraits changed how the Harlem Renaissance is remembered
To describe how the Harmon Foundation chose the artists it commissioned
To provide an overview of Waring’s accomplishments as an educator and a painter
items.explanation: The text first describes Waring’s long teaching career, during which she “established the school’s art and music departments.” It then turns to her painting: she studied in Paris, became “best known for her portraits,” and painted figures such as Marian Anderson and James Weldon Johnson. The text therefore gives an overview of her accomplishments as an educator and a painter, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The text says a scholarship enabled Waring to study in Paris but gives no reason for choosing Paris and makes no comparison with the United States.

B.why_wrong: The text says she painted figures of the Harlem Renaissance, but it does not claim that her portraits changed how that movement is remembered.

C.why_wrong: The Harmon Foundation is mentioned only because it commissioned Waring; the text does not explain how it chose artists.

sources.what: Laura Wheeler Waring (1887–1948): taught at Cheyney for more than thirty years and founded its art and music departments; 1914 Cresson travel scholarship to Paris; Harmon Foundation portraits of prominent African Americans, many Harlem Renaissance figures including Marian Anderson and James Weldon Johnson; portraits in the National Portrait Gallery

items.notes: Area: humanities and arts (painting, education). Key D.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Kathleen Norris’s 1911 novel Mother. Margaret Paget has taught at a small-town school for nearly four years.

She was tired of it all, with an utter and hopeless weariness. Tired of the bells, and the whispering, and the shuffling feet, of the books that smelled of pencil-dust and ink and little dusty fingers; tired of the blackboards, cleaned in great irregular scallops by small and zealous arms; of little girls who sulked. To describe the misbehavior of the students in the classroom where Margaret teaches

items.passage: Musical instruments are traditionally constructed from carefully selected woods and metals, but they can also be assembled from materials most people would discard. <u>In Cateura, a community beside a large landfill in Asunción, Paraguay, a former recycler named Nicolás Gómez has made cellos from oil drums and saxophones from drainpipes</u>. items.passage: Most trees produce their flowers and fruit on new shoots near the ends of their branches. In some species, however, flowers and fruit develop directly on the trunk or on thick, mature branches, a characteristic that botanists call cauliflory. Cauliflory is uncommon in temperate regions but widespread in tropical rainforests. Cacao trees, the source of chocolate, produce their pods along their trunks. The jabuticaba tree of Brazil becomes completely covered in small dark fruits that cling to its bark. And the cannonball tree produces enormous round fruits that dangle from its trunk.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text describes an unusual pattern found in some plants, then gives specific examples of plants that show it.
The text explains why certain plants produce fruit on their trunks, then describes efforts to grow those plants elsewhere.
The text compares trees in temperate and tropical forests, then argues that tropical forests contain more fruit trees.
The text describes a common view about how trees grow, then presents evidence that this view is mistaken.
items.explanation: The first three sentences describe an unusual pattern: in some species, “flowers and fruit develop directly on the trunk or on thick, mature branches,” a characteristic botanists call “cauliflory.” The rest of the text gives examples: cacao, jabuticaba, and the cannonball tree. Choice A describes this structure.

B.why_wrong: The text never explains why these plants fruit on their trunks or mentions efforts to grow them elsewhere.

C.why_wrong: The text says cauliflory is widespread in tropical rainforests, but it does not compare the forests overall or argue that tropical forests have more fruit trees.

D.why_wrong: The first sentence states what most trees do, and the text never calls it mistaken; cauliflory is presented as an exception in some species.

sources.what: Cauliflory: flowering and fruiting from main stems or woody trunks; rare in temperate regions, common in tropical forests; examples include cacao, jackfruit, jabuticaba (Plinia cauliflora), cannonball tree (Couroupita guianensis)

items.notes: Area: natural science (botany). Key A. Avoids the official 1.12 key wording (“describes a general situation, then illustrates that situation with specific examples”).

items.passage: Between 1917 and 1922, the final stretch of the Saw Mill River in Yonkers, New York, was buried in an underground culvert beneath the downtown neighborhood of Getty Square. In the 2010s, the city undertook a project to “daylight” the river, demolishing a parking lot to return the waterway to the surface. The work was completed in phases between 2011 and 2018. The restored river now flows through a park at the center of the neighborhood, and fish such as trout have been observed in the newly uncovered channel.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why Yonkers decided to bury the Saw Mill River in the early 1900s
To explain how a city brought a buried river back to the surface and what has resulted
To argue that other cities should uncover the rivers buried beneath their streets
To compare the cost of uncovering a buried river with the cost of building a new city park
items.explanation: The text explains that the Saw Mill River was buried “beneath the downtown neighborhood of Getty Square” and that Yonkers later “undertook a project to ‘daylight’ the river.” It then gives results: the river “now flows through a park,” and “fish such as trout have been observed in the newly uncovered channel.” Choice B states this purpose.

A.why_wrong: The text says when the river was buried but never explains why, and the burial is only background to the project.

C.why_wrong: The text describes what Yonkers did without urging other cities to do the same.

D.why_wrong: The text never mentions the cost of the project or of building a park.

sources.what: Saw Mill River: last 2,000 feet buried in a culvert under Getty Square 1917–1922; Yonkers daylighting in the 2010s, parking lot removed; phases completed 2011, 2016 and 2018; river is centerpiece of an urban park; fish including trout seen in the daylighted section

items.notes: Area: social science and environment (urban planning). Key B. Key worded away from the official 1.8 key (“an effort ... and some results of that effort”).

items.passage: Before envelopes were common, people often secured letters by folding, tucking, and slitting the paper into a locked packet, a practice now called letterlocking. Researchers have used X-ray scans and computer programs to “flatten” and read damaged documents without opening them. <u>However, these flattening methods had been limited to scrolls, books, and documents with one or two folds</u>. In 2021, a team including conservator Jana Dambrogio developed a method for virtually unfolding intricately locked letters and used it to read a centuries-old letter that had never been opened.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
options: It explains why people eventually stopped using letterlocking.
It describes the steps the 2021 team followed to unfold a letter.
It identifies a shortcoming of earlier methods for reading documents without opening them.
It summarizes what historians have learned from the contents of locked letters.
items.explanation: The sentence before the underlined one says researchers had used scans and programs to read damaged documents “without opening them.” The underlined sentence adds that these methods “had been limited to scrolls, books, and documents with one or two folds,” so they could not handle intricately folded letters. It identifies a shortcoming of the earlier methods, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The text says letterlocking was used before envelopes were common, but the underlined sentence is about modern scanning methods, not why the practice ended.

B.why_wrong: The 2021 team’s method is mentioned only in the last sentence, which does not list its steps; the underlined sentence describes earlier methods.

D.why_wrong: The text never discusses what the letters said or what historians learned from them.

sources.what: Dambrogio et al. 2021, Nature Communications: computational flattening of X-ray microtomography scans had so far been limited to scrolls, books and documents with one or two folds; automatic virtual unfolding of letterlocked letters; contents of one unopened letter read for the first time; letterlocking secured communications for centuries before modern envelopes

items.notes: Area: history and technology (conservation science). Key C (the longest option here; one of the batch's key-longest items, as about one official item in eight). Reading letters without opening them matters because opening destroys the folding evidence (the paper reads letters “while preserving letterlocking evidence”).
